hints: Picture an animal cell next to a bacterial cell side by side - what is the biggest difference in how the inside is organised?
Focus first on the genetic material - where it is held and how it is packaged.
Think about the shape of the DNA molecule itself and any extra small circles of DNA.
Consider internal membranes - which group has separate compartments for different jobs?
Recall the protein-making machinery - both have ribosomes, but how do they differ in size?
Think about the boundary outside the membrane - presence and chemistry of the wall.
Compare how new cells are made in each group for growth and reproduction.
Finish by thinking about body plan - can organisms be made of one cell or many cells?
walkthrough:
Start With the Nucleus - The Defining Split**
You and I can sort almost any cell by asking one question: is the DNA enclosed? In Eukarya the DNA sits inside a nucleus surrounded by a double nuclear envelope with pores. In Bacteria there is no nucleus at all, so the single chromosome lies free in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid.

Compare How DNA Is Built and Packaged**
Next look at the DNA itself. Eukaryotic cells hold several long linear chromosomes, tightly wound around histone proteins to form chromatin. Bacterial cells hold one short circular chromosome, with no histones, plus small extra circles called plasmids. That linear with histones versus circular without histones contrast earns two easy paired marks.

Compare Internal Machinery**
Now think structure determines function. Because Eukarya compartmentalise reactions, they contain membrane-bound organelles: mitochondria and chloroplasts have double membranes, whereas endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi body are bounded by a single membrane. Bacteria have no membrane-bound organelles. Both make proteins with ribosomes, but size matters: 80S in Eukarya and smaller 70S in Bacteria.

Finish With Wall, Division and Body Plan**
Last, look outward and at reproduction. A wall is always present in Bacteria and made of peptidoglycan, while in Eukarya it is only sometimes present and, if present, made of cellulose in plants or chitin in fungi. For cell division, Eukarya use mitosis with spindle and nuclear breakdown, Bacteria use simple binary fission. Linked to this, Eukarya include unicellular and multicellular forms, while Bacteria are unicellular. Write each point as a clear pair to secure all 8 marks.

Final answer: Eukarya have a membrane-bound nucleus / nuclear envelope, Bacteria have no nucleus with DNA free in cytoplasm; Eukarya have linear DNA, Bacteria have circular DNA / plasmids; Eukarya DNA associated with histone proteins, Bacteria DNA has no histones; Eukarya have membrane-bound organelles, Bacteria have none; Eukarya have 80S ribosomes, Bacteria have 70S ribosomes; Eukarya cell wall sometimes present, Bacteria cell wall always present; Eukarya wall (if present) of cellulose / chitin, Bacteria wall of peptidoglycan / murein; Eukarya divide by mitosis, Bacteria divide by binary fission; Eukarya can be multicellular, Bacteria are unicellular.

hints: Remember conservation of plants is often done away from the wild - what places can grow and store rare plants safely?
Think about living collections where whole plants are grown under carefully managed conditions.
Consider how new plants can be made quickly from few parents without seeds.
Think about storing only the seeds, not whole plants - why is that efficient for many years?
Recall what conditions slow down decay and keep seeds alive in storage.
Think about what must be checked and preserved over time to avoid losing variation.
Finish with the long-term goal - how do stored material and knowledge help the wild population?
walkthrough:
Use Botanic Gardens as Living Stores**
Think of ex situ conservation as an ark. Endangered plants are grown in botanic gardens where scientists can control light, water, mineral nutrients and temperature and carry out research. Because only a few individuals may remain, they are multiplied rapidly by propagation such as stem cuttings, tissue culture or controlled pollination, then planted back into the natural environment to rebuild wild populations.

Use Seed Banks as Frozen Gene Banks**
Seeds are ideal because they are small, dormant and genetically diverse. Collections of seeds are stored in seed banks at low temperature with low moisture and low oxygen to reduce respiration and prevent germination or fungal decay. This preserves genetic material and maintains genetic diversity as a gene bank.

Maintain Viability and Return to the Wild**
Stored seeds are regularly tested for viability by germination trials and re-stocked with fresh seeds when viability falls. When habitat is restored, seeds can be germinated in nurseries prior to introduction back into the natural habitat. This ex situ work is backed by in situ projects such as removing alien species or forestry protection, and by international agreements such as CITES that control trade in endangered species.

Final answer: Grow in botanic gardens under controlled conditions of light, water, nutrients and temperature for research and propagation by cuttings, tissue culture or controlled pollination, then plant back into natural habitat; collect and store seeds in seed banks at low temperature, low moisture and low oxygen, regularly test viability and re-stock, acting as gene bank to preserve genetic diversity; germinate seeds before reintroduction; support in situ projects and legislation such as CITES.
